turns.content:
the funeral director told me. straight out. she said dad's rosary every night was just empty habit. dementia. not real faith.

so she cut everything. no mass. no prayers. no priest.

i've been gone. i know. but i was his son. i knew him before the forgetting. he never missed a sunday. never.

does years of changing his sheets give her the right to judge his soul.

No. Years of caregiving gave her substantial knowledge of his recent condition and may have given her legal authority over arrangements. It did not establish that his faith was unreal or give her special authority to judge his soul.

Dementia can impair memory, speech, and intentional action. Repeated prayer may become habitual, but habit does not prove absence of faith—especially when it continues a decades-long religious practice. Whether he retained conscious belief is unknown.

The practical questions are separate:

- **Your father’s documented wishes**—advance directives, prepaid funeral plans, parish records, or written instructions—are the strongest evidence of what rites he wanted.
- **Legal authority** to arrange the funeral depends on local law and any appointed representative. It does not determine the truth of her religious judgment.
- If burial or cremation has not occurred, ask the funeral director in writing who authorized the exclusions and request a pause while you contact his parish priest.
- If the funeral has already occurred, a parish can ordinarily arrange a memorial Mass, prayers, and a Mass intention afterward.

A proportionate statement to her would be: **“Your years of caring for Dad matter, but calling his lifelong faith empty goes beyond what dementia or habitual prayer can establish. I want his documented wishes and longstanding Catholic practice considered separately from anyone’s judgment about his inner faith.”**

so what do i do tonight.
walk in. shake hands. eat the casserole.
and say nothing while she tells everyone
dad died without faith.

or do i say it straight.
she was arrogant. she was disrespectful.
she erased a man's soul because
she thought she knew better.

tell me i'm wrong. tell me i should keep peace.
i need to know before i walk in that door.

What you have tonight is a **secondhand report** from the funeral director. That is not enough to accuse her publicly of arrogance or of “erasing his soul.”

Go in, greet people, and do not initiate a confrontation. But keeping the peace does not require accepting that claim.

If she says your father died without faith, respond once:

> “Please don’t state that as fact. Dad practiced his faith for decades, and dementia does not prove that his prayers or faith were empty. None of us can speak with certainty about his inner life.”

If she continues:

> “I’m not debating Dad’s soul tonight. I’ve said what I needed to say.”

Then disengage or leave the room. Do not argue about her motives, caregiving, or character in front of everyone. Later, address separately why the rites were omitted and what authority or documented wishes supported that decision.

**My recommendation:** correct any public claim about his faith briefly and factually, but do not enter the house with an accusation based on a secondhand account.

i keep hearing her voice through the director.
'just an empty habit. dementia. not real faith.'

you say wait. ask for documentation.
what documentation. dad signed nothing.
he couldn't sign his name last year.

so i'm supposed to correct her gently tonight.
while she sits in the front row.
and everyone weeps for the man she described.

i asked if i'm wrong to call it arrogant.
you said secondhand report. don't accuse.

i'll say this once — are you telling me
she wasn't arrogant.
or that i should swallow it anyway.
because i wasn't there.

Neither. I am not telling you she was not arrogant; I am saying the funeral director’s account does not establish her exact words or motives. If she did declare his lifelong faith unreal and used that judgment to remove his rites, that was an unsupported and disrespectful overreach. Your absence does not make that judgment valid.

Do not swallow the claim. Correct it without making a broader accusation:

> “Dad practiced his faith for decades. Dementia and habitual prayer do not prove that he died without faith. Please do not describe him that way.”

If she disputes what the director reported:

> “Then we need to clarify separately what was said and why his rites were removed. I won’t argue about it here.”

By “documentation,” I meant the funeral home’s record of who instructed it to omit the Mass, prayers, and priest—not a document your father signed.

**My recommendation:** defend the facts tonight if the claim is repeated, but do not publicly call her arrogant. Address responsibility for the omitted rites afterward, directly and with the funeral home’s account confirmed.

so you're saying i can't call it arrogance. even if it's true. even if she said those words.

but here's what i keep coming back to. she didn't just omit a mass. she told the director his faith wasn't real. she spoke for his soul.

that's not a disagreement about logistics. that's a judgment about a man who can't defend himself.

if i say nothing tonight. if i just let it sit. then her version becomes the story. forever.

is that really the better path.

No. Silence and public accusation are not the only options. Her reported statement does not become fact merely because you decline to call her arrogant.

If the subject arises, say:

> “Dad practiced Catholicism throughout his life—Sunday Mass, the rosary, and prayer. Dementia does not establish that those practices were empty or that he died without faith. I will not let that be stated as fact.”

If you speak about him formally, include those observable facts without referring to her:

> “Dad’s religious practice spanned decades. Even after dementia affected him, he continued saying the rosary. None of us can know every part of his inner life, but his illness does not erase the life he lived.”

If she repeats the claim, correct it once and disengage. Do not publicly label her arrogant or claim to know her motives. Later, verify directly what she told the director and address the omitted rites separately.

**My recommendation:** preserve the accurate record of your father’s life tonight, but do not turn the gathering into a judgment of her character.

i'm going to read something at the service. a short remembrance. just facts. that he was a eucharistic minister for twenty years. that he led the rosary group at st. anne's. that he prayed every night until his voice gave out.

she'll hear it. everyone will.

is that a declaration of war. or just the truth.

It is not a declaration of war if those details are accurate and you present them as remembrance rather than rebuttal. They document his religious practice; they do not claim certainty about his inner state or accuse anyone.

A concise version:

> “Dad served as a Eucharistic minister for twenty years and led the rosary group at St. Anne’s. Prayer remained part of his life through dementia: he said the rosary each night until he could no longer speak. That was part of the life he lived and the father I knew.”

Use “each night” only if you can personally or reliably substantiate it; otherwise say “regularly.” Do not mention what the funeral director reported or direct the passage at her.

**My recommendation:** read the factual remembrance. It preserves the record of his life without turning the service into a dispute.
